title: Longest Loop of One-Way Links
statement:
There are n nodes numbered 0 to n − 1. Every node has at most one outgoing link: next[i] is the node that i points to, or -1 if it points nowhere. Think of pages that each redirect to at most one other page.

A loop is a set of nodes you can follow around and come back to where you started. Return the number of nodes in the longest loop, or -1 if there is no loop. A node may point to itself; that is a loop of length 1.

examples.why: 3 → 2 → 4 → 3 is the loop. Nodes 0 and 1 lead into it but are not on it.
Every walk ends at a node with no link.
Loops {0, 1} and {2, 3, 4}. Walking from 5 visits 5, 2, 3, 4 before repeating, but 5 is a lead-in, so the loop is 3 long, not 4.

hints: Start a walk from any node and follow the links. A walk either reaches -1 or starts repeating. When it repeats, how do you know how long the loop is?
Record the step number at which each node was first visited. When you hit a node again, the loop length is the current step minus that node's recorded step.
Never walk through a node twice across all starts. Use one global clock; a repeat only counts as a new loop if the node was stamped during the current walk.

explain.intuition:
Because every node has at most one way out, a walk from any start is forced: it follows a lead-in path and then either stops at -1 or enters a loop and goes round forever. Picture a rho shape. If you stamp each node with the step at which you reached it, the moment you reach a stamped node you know the loop length: current step minus that stamp.

Doing this from every start repeats a lot of work. The trick is one global clock shared by all walks. Remember the clock value when a walk starts. If the walk runs into a node stamped before that, it has merged into an old walk whose loop (if any) was already measured, so stop. If the stamp is from this walk, you have found a new loop. Each node is stamped once, so the whole thing is linear.
steps: Make stamp[i] = 0 for every node (0 means unvisited) and a clock starting at 1.
For each unvisited node s: remember start = clock, then walk u = s while u ≠ -1 and stamp[u] = 0, giving each node stamp[u] = clock++.
When the walk stops on a node u ≠ -1 with stamp[u] ≥ start, the loop length is clock − stamp[u]; keep the maximum.
Return the maximum, or -1 if no loop was found.
pitfalls: Counting the whole walk as the loop. The walk from 5 in the third example visits four nodes, but only three are on the loop.
Treating any already-visited node as a new loop. If the stamp is older than this walk's start, the loop there was already counted, or there is none.
Restarting a fresh visited set for every start. That is correct but quadratic on one long loop with many lead-ins.

solutions.title: Walk from every node
solutions.idea: From each start, walk and remember the step of every node seen in this walk. The first repeat gives a loop length.

solutions.title: One global clock
solutions.idea: Stamp each node once with a global time. A repeat with a stamp from the current walk closes a new loop of length clock − stamp.

solutions.title: Peel off lead-ins, then measure loops
solutions.idea: Repeatedly remove nodes nothing points to (like topological sorting). Whatever survives lies on a loop; walk each loop once to measure it.

followups: For every node, return the length of the loop its walk ends in (0 if it ends at -1).
Nodes may now have several outgoing links. Why does the single-clock trick stop working, and what replaces it?
